:::{#def-generalized-inverse}
#### Generalized inverse

A **generalized inverse** of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$
is an $n \times m$ matrix $\matr{G}$ such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{m \times n}\,
\underbrace{\matr{G}}_{n \times m}\,
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{m \times n}
= \matr{A}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-generalized-inverse}
#### A matrix with many generalized inverses

Let $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
and $\matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ g_{21} & g_{22} \end{bmatrix}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{A} \matr{G} \matr{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-mult, for } \matr{A} \matr{G} \text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} g_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
&& \text{(@def-matrix-mult)}
\ea
$$

which equals $\matr{A}$ exactly when $g_{11} = 1$.
So every matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & g_{12} \\ g_{21} & g_{22} \end{bmatrix}$
is a generalized inverse of $\matr{A}$:
a generalized inverse need not be unique.
The zero matrix is not one, since its $(1, 1)$ entry is $0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-generalized-inverse-invertible}
#### An invertible matrix has only one generalized inverse

If $\matr{A}$ is an invertible $p \times p$ matrix (@def-invertible-matrix),
its only generalized inverse is $\matr{A}^{-1}$.

:::

::: proof

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A} \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{A} &= \matr{I}_p \matr{A} \\
&= \matr{A}
\end{aligned}
$$

(@def-matrix-inverse, @thm-identity),
so $\matr{A}^{-1}$ is a generalized inverse.
If $\matr{G}$ is any generalized inverse, then

$$
\ba
\matr{G}
&= \matr{I}_p\,\matr{G}\,\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\\
&= (\matr{A}^{-1} \matr{A})\,\matr{G}\,(\matr{A} \matr{A}^{-1})
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^{-1}\,(\matr{A} \matr{G} \matr{A})\,\matr{A}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{A} \matr{A}^{-1}
&& \text{(@def-generalized-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p\,\matr{A}^{-1}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^{-1}.
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-generalized-inverse-invertible}
#### The generalized inverse of an invertible matrix

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
of @exm-invertible-matrix,
the only generalized inverse is
$\matr{A}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
The matrix of @exm-generalized-inverse, by contrast, has infinitely many,
so by @thm-generalized-inverse-invertible it is singular.

:::
